title: Chain — the starting line and the spacer
subtitle: Foundation chain, turning chain, and the chains inside patterns all work differently
excerpt: The chain is the first move every crocheter learns — and the most underestimated. The starting chain, the turning chain, and in-pattern chain spaces all behave differently. This tutorial covers all three.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776 — the starting chain as the foundation for all crochet pieces. Weldon's Practical Crochet, Vol. 1 (1886) — turning chains and their varying counts by stitch type.

glossaryTerms.definition: The starting row of chains that acts as the base for a flat crochet piece. The number of chains determines the width of the first row.
A gap created by one or more chains between two stitches. In motifs and lace, stitches are often worked into the chain space rather than into individual stitches.
The short chain at the start of each new row that brings the working yarn to the height of the stitch being worked. Whether it counts as a stitch depends on the stitch type.

content.text: The chain does three different jobs in crochet — and which job it's doing changes how you work into it. The
foundation chain
is the starting base. The
turning chain
lifts the working yarn to row height at the start of each new row. The in-pattern chain creates a
chain space
that later stitches work into. Understanding the difference avoids the most common chain errors.
Anatomy of a chain

Each chain link has three surfaces. The front shows a V shape — two loops, one on top of the other. The back shows a single bump (called the back bump or the third loop). When you work stitches into a foundation chain for the first row, you usually go under both top loops of the V. Working into the back bump only leaves the V intact on the surface and gives a neater, stretchier starting edge.
The foundation chain
Every flat crochet piece starts with a foundation chain. The number of chains determines the width. Count the chains without the slip knot and without the loop currently on the hook.
Make a slip knot. Slide onto the hook.
Yarn over — wrap the working yarn over the hook from back to front.
Pull the yarn through the loop on the hook. One new chain made. One loop remains on the hook.
Repeat for the number of chains the pattern specifies.
Do not count the loop on the hook as a chain. Do not count the slip knot as a chain.

attrs.title: How tight is right
attrs.body: Foundation chains that are too tight pull the first row hard and make it difficult to insert the hook cleanly. A common trick: use a hook one size larger for the foundation chain only, then switch to the pattern hook for row 1. The chain stays loose and even.

content.text: The turning chain

At the start of each new row you chain up to the height of the stitch you're about to work. The number of turning chains and whether they count as a stitch is the most argued detail in crochet patterns.

Standard turning chain counts: ch 1 for double crochet (does not count as a stitch); ch 2 for half treble (counts or doesn't — check the pattern); ch 3 for treble (counts as the first treble); ch 4 for double treble; ch 5 for triple treble. When a turning chain counts as a stitch, you skip the first stitch at the base of the chain and work into the second stitch. When it doesn't count, work into the first stitch at the base.
Chain spaces in patterns

A chain space is a gap left between two stitches where later stitches work into the gap rather than into individual stitches. In granny-square patterns, the corner is a ch-2 space that holds a whole cluster. In lace patterns, a ch-5 arch becomes the base for the next row of stitches.
Work to the point where the pattern says 'ch N'.
Make the stated number of chains.
Skip the stated number of stitches beneath the chain (the pattern will tell you how many to skip).
Continue the row as stated. On the following row or round, stitches work into the chain space — push the hook under all the chains to work into the gap.

items.symptom: Foundation chain too tight to work into
items.cause: Gripping the chain too firmly and working close to the tip of the hook
items.fix: Work the chain higher up on the hook where the shaft is wider, or use a hook one size larger for the chain only.

items.symptom: Row count is off after several rows
items.cause: Counting the turning chain as a stitch when it shouldn't be, or vice versa
items.fix: Check the pattern's turning chain note at the start of the first pattern row. Mark the first stitch of each row with a stitch marker.

items.symptom: Work gets wider row by row
items.cause: Working into the turning chain at the end of the return row when it isn't a stitch
items.fix: At the end of each row, check whether the last stitch goes into the turning chain from the previous row. If the turning chain doesn't count as a stitch, skip it.

content.text: What to try next

The chainless foundation treble eliminates the separate foundation chain entirely — it builds the first row as it chains up. Worth learning for any blanket or garment where the lower edge needs to stretch.
